summary: Read the spec, the plan, src/serve.mjs and test/serve.test.mjs cold. In a throwaway worktree I fuzzed resolvePublic with 300k random combinations of '..', '.', %2e/%2E, %2f, %5c, backslash, %00, lone '%', %25, overlong %c0%ae, '//', '?', '#' and spaces, all on POSIX: it never threw and never returned a path outside <root>/public, and it never returned public/ itself. Decode-once, malformed escapes, NUL, backslash, a sibling with the same prefix (public-secret) and the root itself all hold. The categories about transactions, concurrency, retries and ordering do not apply: this is a pure, synchronous function. I proved no attacks. Unproven ideas, one per line: (1) Windows only, tested by mocking node:path with path.win32: '/..%20/x' resolves to public\.. \x and '/.../x' to public\...\x. The check passes them, and if Win32 path normalization strips trailing spaces or dots from '.. ' or reads '...' as a parent, they could escape. I could not prove this without a Windows filesystem. (2) Windows: 'C:' and '/C:x' are accepted as public\C: and public\C:x, and '/index.html::$DATA' and '/CON' are accepted (alternate data streams and device names). These are not containment escapes, but the filesystem may read them differently from the check (FM-4). (3) A query string or fragment ('/index.html?v=1', '%3f') becomes part of the filename. That is HTTP handling, which the spec puts out of scope. (4) A root that is not a string makes path.resolve throw. The root is not request input, so this does not break AC-4. (5) Symlinks inside public/ that point outside it are not checked. Serving files is out of scope.
